books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: James K. Polk, Special Message to Congress, May 11, 1846
John C. Calhoun, Senate resolutions, February 19, 1847
Constitution of the State of California, Article I, Section 18, 1849
Reynolds's Political Map of the United States, 1856

source: original; documents are public-domain primary sources (see each document's sourcing note)
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the Mexican-American War changed the debate over slavery in the United States in the period 1846–1856.

documents.title: Polk asks Congress for war
documents.source: James K. Polk, Special Message to Congress, May 11, 1846. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Polk, the Democratic president, asking Congress to declare war on Mexico two days before it did so.
documents.text: Mexico has passed the boundary of the United States, has invaded our territory and shed American blood upon the American soil. She has proclaimed that hostilities have commenced, and that the two nations are now at war. As war exists, and, notwithstanding all our efforts to avoid it, exists by the act of Mexico herself, we are called upon by every consideration of duty and patriotism to vindicate with decision the honor, the rights, and the interests of our country.

documents.title: The Wilmot Proviso
documents.source: Wilmot Proviso, amendment offered by David Wilmot (D-PA) to an appropriations bill, August 8, 1846. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Wilmot, a Democratic congressman from Pennsylvania, offering his amendment during the war itself.
documents.text: Provided, That, as an express and fundamental condition to the acquisition of any territory from the Republic of Mexico by the United States, by virtue of any treaty which may be negotiated between them, and to the use by the Executive of the moneys herein appropriated, neither slavery nor involuntary servitude shall ever exist in any part of said territory, except for crime, whereof the party shall first be duly convicted.

documents.title: Wilmot defends his Proviso
documents.source: David Wilmot, speech in the House of Representatives, February 8, 1847 (Congressional Globe, 29th Congress, 2nd session, Appendix, p. 315). Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Wilmot, defending his Proviso on the House floor six months after offering it, speaking to Northerners and Southerners alike.
documents.text: But, sir, the issue now presented is not whether slavery shall exist unmolested where it now is, but whether it shall be carried to new and distant regions, now free, where the footprint of a slave cannot be found. This, sir, is the issue. Upon it I take my stand, and from it I cannot be frightened or driven by idle charges of abolitionism. I ask not that slavery be abolished, I demand that this government preserve the integrity of free territory against the aggressions of slavery — against its wrongful usurpations. . . . Now, sir, we are told that California is ours, that New Mexico is ours — won by the valor of our arms. They are free. Shall they remain free? Shall these fair provinces be the inheritance and homes of the white labor of freemen or the black labor of slaves? This, sir, is the issue.

documents.title: Calhoun's resolutions on the territories
documents.source: John C. Calhoun, resolutions offered in the Senate, February 19, 1847. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Calhoun, the South Carolina senator and defender of slavery, answering the Wilmot Proviso with a constitutional claim about the territories.
documents.text: Resolved, That the territories of the United States belong to the several States composing this Union, and are held by them as their joint and common property. Resolved, That Congress, as the joint agent and representative of the States of this Union, has no right to make any law, or do any act whatever, that shall directly, or by its effects, make any discrimination between the States of this Union, by which any of them shall be deprived of its full and equal right in any territory of the United States, acquired or to be acquired.

documents.title: The Free-Soil platform at Buffalo
documents.source: Free-Soil Party platform, adopted at Buffalo, New York, August 9, 1848. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The platform of the new Free-Soil Party, written by former Democrats, Liberty men, and Conscience Whigs who had bolted their parties over slavery's expansion.
documents.text: Resolved, That we inscribe on our banner, “Free Soil, Free Speech, Free Labor, and Free Men,” and under it we will fight on, and fight ever, until a triumphant victory shall reward our exertions. Resolved, That in the judgment of this Convention, Congress has no more power to make a Slave than to make a King; no more power to institute or establish Slavery than to institute or establish a Monarchy.

documents.title: California's constitution bans slavery
documents.source: Constitution of the State of California, Article I, Section 18, adopted 1849. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The constitution written by California's own convention at Monterey in 1849, as the territory rushed toward statehood.
documents.text: Neither slavery, nor involuntary servitude, unless for the punishment of crimes, shall ever be tolerated in this State.

documents.title: Reynolds's Political Map of the United States
documents.source: Reynolds's Political Map of the United States, published by Wm. C. Reynolds, New York, 1856. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A Republican campaign map for the 1856 election, with portraits of Frémont and Dayton at the top, designed to show the comparative area of the free and slave states.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which the development in question occurred, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of change does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the annexation of Texas, Manifest Destiny, or the sectional balance before the war.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant evidence from at least three documents to support an argument about the prompt.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than three documents, or quoting documents without describing what they show, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support an argument, with the evidence accurately described and tied to the claim.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example beyond the documents, such as the Compromise of 1850, the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854, or the Dred Scott decision of 1857.
rubric.notEarned: A general statement with no specific example beyond the documents does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document's author, purpose, audience, or historical situation to the argument, for at least two documents.
rubric.notEarned: Identifying an author without explaining why it matters, or sourcing only one document, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for demonstrating a complex understanding, such as qualifying the extent of change, explaining why the change was limited, or showing how the same development pulled in opposite directions.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: The Mexican-American War transformed the slavery debate from a question about slavery where it already existed into a question about slavery in new lands, and that shift broke the old party system — though the argument itself, North against South, was older than the war.
Context: By 1846 Texas was annexed, Oregon was settled with Britain, and Polk's war with Mexico was about to add California and the Southwest.
Evidence: Documents 1-3 show the war producing the slavery question — Polk's war message, Wilmot's ban, and Wilmot's defense of it. Documents 4-6 show the answers splitting apart — Calhoun's claim that Congress could not ban slavery in common territory, the Free-Soil Party's new banner, and California banning slavery in its own constitution. Document 7 shows the result on a map: a Republican campaign poster weighing free against slave land.
Beyond the documents: The Compromise of 1850 admitted California free and left the rest of the Cession to popular sovereignty, and the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 repealed the Missouri Compromise line outright.
Sourcing: Polk wrote as a president asking for war; Wilmot spoke as a Northern Democrat defending his own amendment; Calhoun wrote as a Southern senator stating a constitutional theory; the Reynolds map was a partisan poster for a Republican ticket.
Complexity: The war changed the question more than the sides — the sections had disagreed before, but the new lands gave the disagreement a map, a party, and a deadline.
